titre: Mincome: What a Guaranteed Minimum Income Changed in Dauphin (1974-1979)
accroche: From 1974 to 1979, Dauphin, Manitoba, tests a guaranteed income for everyone. No one analyzes the results, until a researcher reopens the file.
contenu_vulgarise:
In February 1974, the governments of Manitoba and Canada launch an unprecedented experiment in Dauphin, a town of about 10,000 people: for five years, every family earning less than a certain threshold receives a guaranteed income supplement, with no conditions on employment or behavior, a “Mincome,” short for minimum income. Unlike the other parts of the experiment, run in Winnipeg and in rural Manitoba on a randomly drawn sample, Dauphin is treated as a “saturation site”: its entire population is eligible, which makes it possible to observe the effects of a guaranteed income on a whole community rather than on isolated households surrounded by neighbors who do not receive it.

## A Net That Tightens as Earned Income Rises

The principle is that of a negative income tax: a family with no income receives the full guarantee, set according to its size; each dollar earned elsewhere then reduces this aid by 35, 50, or 75 cents depending on the variant tested, so that working always remains more advantageous than not working. The experiment ends in 1979, when the provincial and federal governments, both now in conservative hands (Sterling Lyon in Manitoba, Joe Clark in Ottawa), do not renew it. No in-depth analysis is published at the time: the data pile up without any research budget to fund their processing, and the experiment falls into oblivion for nearly thirty years.

## What Hospital Records Ended Up Showing

It is the economist Evelyn Forget, of the University of Manitoba, who reopens the file in the 2000s: not by going back to the raw Mincome data themselves, but by comparing, over the period of the experiment, Dauphin's hospital statistics with those of comparable Manitoba towns that stayed outside the program. The result: an 8.5% drop in the hospitalization rate in Dauphin during the Mincome years, driven notably by accidents, work-related injuries, and psychiatric hospitalizations. Among teenagers, the number completing secondary school rises, a sign that the guaranteed income allowed some to stay in school rather than go to work earlier. And on the point that worried the politicians of the day most (the idea that a guaranteed income would make people stop working), Forget finds practically no effect, with two exceptions: mothers of newborns and teenagers, who reduce their time in paid work, the former to care for their child, the latter to stay in school. Thirty years after the experiment ended, it was hospital records, not the reports it was meant to produce, that finally answered the question it posed.

repere.texte: During the five years of Mincome, the hospitalization rate in Dauphin fell by 8.5% compared with similar Manitoba towns, according to Evelyn Forget's retrospective analysis.

carte.punch: A Canadian town tested a guaranteed income for five years, never analyzing it at the time.
carte.idee: From 1974 to 1979, Dauphin, Manitoba, tests a guaranteed minimum income for all its residents. The experiment ends without being analyzed; thirty years later, Evelyn Forget compares its hospital records with those of neighboring towns and documents 8.5% fewer hospitalizations.

quiz.question: Why is Dauphin, unlike the other sites of the Mincome experiment, called a “saturation site”?
choix: Because only randomly drawn residents received the guaranteed income there
Because its entire population was eligible for the guaranteed income, not just a sample
Because the town already had a minimum income before the experiment
Because it had more residents than Winnipeg
quiz.explication: In Winnipeg and rural Manitoba, only a randomly drawn sample received the guaranteed income; in Dauphin, the whole population was entitled to it, which made it possible to observe the effects on a whole community rather than on isolated households.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the Mincome benefit decrease when a family earns income elsewhere?
choix: It stays the same, whatever the income earned
It falls by 35, 50, or 75 cents per dollar earned, depending on the variant tested
It automatically doubles once the family exceeds the poverty line
It is eliminated entirely from the first dollar earned
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry describes a negative income tax in which the benefit falls by 35, 50, or 75 cents per dollar earned depending on the variant, so that working always remains more advantageous than not working.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What effect does Evelyn Forget document on teenagers' schooling in Dauphin?
choix: A drop in the number of teenagers enrolled in school
No measurable effect on teenagers' schooling
A rise in the number of teenagers completing secondary school
A legal requirement to stay in school until age 18
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that the number of teenagers completing secondary school rises during the Mincome years, an effect documented by Forget, with no legal requirement and no drop.
